study.title: Completion queues: how the NIC tells you work is done
study.big_idea: When the network card finishes a job, it leaves a short note in a shared list in memory, and your program checks that list instead of waiting for the operating system to tell it.
background: What you need to know first, explained from scratch.
A second paragraph that builds on the first.
steps: The app writes a work request describing what to send.
The app rings the doorbell: one write that tells the NIC there's new work.
The NIC does the work and writes a completion entry into the completion queue.
The app polls the queue, sees the entry and knows the job is done.
study.example: A concrete, practical scenario that shows the idea working.
study.why_xlio: XLIO polls completion queues from user space instead of waiting on interrupts and the kernel.
study.pitfall: A common misconception, and why it's wrong.
terms: Network interface card: the hardware that sends and receives network packets.
study.question: Why can several connections share one completion queue?
study.answer: Each completion entry says which connection it belongs to, so one polling loop can serve many connections.
